items.scenario: Your boss asks if you have sent the report to the client yet. You reply by work email, politely.
items.explain: In a work email, 'send' is neutral and clear. 'Shoot over' is casual, for friends. 'Ship' usually means releasing a product.

items.scenario: You text a close friend: you want them to send yesterday's photo quickly.
items.explain: 'Shoot over' is very casual and quick, for friends or close colleagues. 'Submit' and 'dispatch' sound formal or mechanical.

items.scenario: You write an email asking your manager to approve travel expenses. Formal tone.
items.explain: 'Request' is formal and suits work documents. 'Want' is too direct, 'gimme' is very casual and not for a manager.

items.scenario: You arrive at a meeting 10 minutes late. You say it to your manager as you enter.
items.explain: 'Sorry' is the safe choice with a superior. 'My bad' is light, for equal colleagues. 'Oops' is only for a small slip, said quietly.

items.scenario: Internal announcement: the tech team has just released a new version of the app.
items.explain: At work, 'ship' means releasing a product to market. 'Mail' means sending letters, 'deliver' means handing goods to a customer.

items.scenario: Scholarship application, family section: you need to mention your children. Formal tone.
items.explain: 'Children' is formal and used in official documents. 'Kids' is more casual, 'babies' only refers to very young children.

items.scenario: The company's official notice of a new policy: customers can purchase products through the website.
items.explain: 'Purchase' is formal, used in official documents. 'Buy' is more neutral, 'grab' means buying quickly and is very casual.

items.scenario: You tell friends about the big fish you just caught, excited.
items.explain: 'Huge' is used when excited, in everyday talk. 'Big' is neutral and general. 'Vast' usually describes wide spaces like seas or plains.

items.scenario: In your report: the new rule will affect employees' salaries.
items.explain: 'Affect' is a verb meaning to have an influence on. 'Effect' is usually a noun (result, impact), so it is easy to confuse. 'Involve' means include or require, not influence.

items.scenario: You message your group: you want to know who will join tonight. Friendly tone.
items.explain: 'Let me know' is friendly and common at work and in messages. 'Inform me' is too formal, like an official notice. 'Tell me' is a bit blunt.
